---
title: "Safety without lifetimes"
---

Jestyr's memory safety is a mosaic, not a monolith. Four tiers, each with a
precise promise and a named enforcer. You pick the tier per data structure, and
the compiler holds you to it. There are no lifetime annotations anywhere in the
language — not because inference got smarter, but because the design removed
the thing annotations describe.

| Tier | Promise | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| values + second-class borrows | a borrow cannot outlive its frame | compile error (escape checker) |
| `genref` (`&T`) | use-after-free is a deterministic runtime fault, never UB | generation check on every deref |
| `region` (`&[r]T`) | zero-cost refs confined to their arena's scope | compile error |
| `unsafe` | nothing checked — a written contract you sign lexically | required block; uncovered raw-pointer ops are compile errors |

## Tier 1: values, and borrows that only flow down

The default is ownership by value: moves transfer, and scope exit runs RAII
drops — recursively, into owned struct fields and live enum payloads
(`examples/drop_nested.jtr`).

References are **second-class borrows**: parameter conventions `read`, `mut`,
and `out`. A borrow can be passed further down the call stack, but it cannot be
returned by value, stored, or given away. That single restriction is the whole
trick. Rust proves "this reference outlives that one" with named lifetimes;
Jestyr makes the question unaskable — a callee's frame always ends before its
caller's, so a borrow that only flows down is valid by the call stack's own
discipline. There is nothing left to infer, so there is nothing to annotate.

The escape checker walks every function body and refuses exactly four escape
routes — the only ways a value leaves a frame:

```{.rust}
struct Node   { value: i32 }
struct Holder { inner: i32 }

// ✗ route 1 — return: the borrow would outlive the call
fn leak(read p: Node) -> Node {
    p
}

// ✗ route 2 — capture: stored in a struct value that may outlive the frame
fn capture(read p: Node) -> Holder {
    Holder{ inner: p }
}

// ✗ route 3 — store: written into caller-owned storage
fn stash(read p: Node, mut h: Holder) {
    h.inner = p
}

// route 4 — give-away: passing a borrow to a `take` (owning) parameter,
// which is how `vec.push(borrow)` is caught (examples/collection.jtr).

// ✓ flowing DOWN is always safe — the callee's frame is strictly inner
fn ok_forward(read p: Node) {
    consume(p)
}

// ✓ and a signature may opt into handing a borrow back out
fn ok_borrow_out(read p: Node) -> read Node {
    p
}
```

The compiler's actual output on that file:

::: {.program-output}
```
error: cannot return borrow `p`: a second-class `read`/`mut`/`out` borrow may
       not outlive its call (pass it further down, or declare the return as
       `read`/`mut`/`out`)
  --> examples/escapes.jtr:11:5

error: cannot store borrow `p` in struct `Holder`: a second-class borrow may
       not outlive its call
  --> examples/escapes.jtr:16:20
   = help: a stored value must outlive the call: pass it as `take` to transfer
     ownership, allocate it in a `region` if it must outlive this frame, or
     store a `genref` handle instead of a borrow

error: cannot store borrow `p` into borrowed storage: it would outlive its call
  --> examples/escapes.jtr:21:5

3 error(s)
```
:::

Note what the help text does: each rejection names the tier that solves the
problem legitimately. That is the mosaic working as a system.

::: {.claim}
**For every program the checker accepts, no second-class borrow is usable
after the frame that introduced it has returned.** Scope: checked code and
second-class borrows; lifetime safety, not aliasing races (`mut` borrows are
exclusive by convention, and shared-memory concurrency goes through `Mutex`
and channels). Precise statement and the exhaustiveness argument:
[docs/escape-guarantee.md](https://github.com/AdamEzzat1/Jestyr/blob/master/docs/escape-guarantee.md).
<span class="verify">$ jestyrc check examples/escapes.jtr</span>
:::

## Tier 2: genref — storable handles, checked derefs

Borrows can't build a graph or a cache: those need references that *outlive
frames*. That is `genref` (`&T`): a copyable, storable `{ptr, generation}`
pair. Each allocation carries a generation; the reference snapshots it; every
deref compares the snapshot against the live generation.

```{.rust}
fn main() -> i32 {
    var r: &i32 = gen_new(i32, 42)
    print_int(r.* as i64)   // generation matches → safe deref
    gen_free(r)             // bumps the generation
    print_int(r.* as i64)   // faults, deterministically — never UB
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
42
Assertion failed!

Program: jestyr_uaf.exe
File: uaf.jtr, Line 5
:::

That second line is the whole point: the use-after-free stops the program at
the exact source line that did it, instead of silently returning whatever now
occupies the freed memory.

The promise is deliberately weaker than tier 1 and deliberately stronger than
a raw pointer: use-after-free is not prevented at compile time, but it is a
**deterministic runtime fault** — never a silent read of freed memory, never
undefined behaviour for gcc to optimize around.

## Tier 3: region — zero-cost arena refs

The zero-cost tier. A `region r { … }` block owns a bump arena;
`region_alloc(r, T, v)` returns a `&[r]T` — a plain pointer with **no
per-deref check**. Safety is lexical instead: a `&[r]T` cannot leave the
region's scope, and the whole arena is freed in O(1) at the closing brace.

```{.rust}
region r {
    var a: &[r]i32 = region_alloc(r, i32, 10)
    print_int(a.*)    // raw deref — zero runtime cost
}                     // whole arena freed here, at once
```

Escaping is a compile error, with the same tier-aware help:

::: {.program-output}
```
error: cannot return region-allocated value `g`: it is owned by its `region`
       arena and does not outlive it (copy it into an owned `String` to
       return it)
  --> examples/region_escape.jtr:14:16
```
:::

::: {.claim}
A `&[r]T` cannot leave its region's scope; the demo file is refused with two
errors. Scope: compile-time rejection, both toolchains.
<span class="verify">$ jestyrc check examples/region_escape.jtr</span>
:::

## Tier 4: unsafe — enforced, and written down

Raw pointers (`*mut T`, `*const T`) exist for what remains: FFI, MMIO,
allocator internals, and the disjoint-write sharing pattern behind
`par_binned_sum`. And `unsafe` is **fully enforced**: dereferencing,
doing arithmetic on, or manufacturing a raw pointer outside an `unsafe` block
is a compile error — on the Rust reference *and* the self-hosted compiler.
This wasn't always true; the enforcement ladder (report → contract →
migration → warn → error) was staged so that flipping to error broke nothing:
the corpus was migrated to zero uncovered sites first, out of an original
census of 171 raw-pointer sites.

What `unsafe` buys is not a free-for-all but a *lexical obligation*: the
[written contract](https://github.com/AdamEzzat1/Jestyr/blob/master/docs/unsafe-contract.md) specifies deref validity,
pointer provenance (including the int-to-pointer MMIO door and `@volatile`),
the aliasing assumptions the block must preserve, the C-interop boundary, and
the rule that a sound block restores every invariant it suspends by its
closing brace. `jestyrc unsafe <file>` reports every raw-pointer operation
and whether a block covers it.

::: {.claim}
Uncovered raw-pointer operations are compile errors on both toolchains; the
report tool and the diagnostic share one collector, so they cannot drift.
Scope: raw deref, raw arithmetic, and int-to-pointer casts.
<span class="verify">$ jestyrc unsafe examples/std/cgen.jtr</span>
:::

## Does it hold up at scale?

The compiler is written in Jestyr, so the discipline is tested against the
largest program the language has: **the self-hosted compiler plus its stdlib
is 29,818 lines of Jestyr containing 162 mentions of `unsafe` — 0.5%.** The
two biggest modules make the shape concrete: `cgen.jtr` is 14,499 lines with
5 unsafe sites; `typeck.jtr` is 2,859 lines with 3. The flattened compiler
passes the escape checker with zero diagnostics and self-hosts to a
byte-identical fixed point.

The safe tiers are not the slow path, either. `heavy_wordcount` — 10 million
words hashed into `std/strmap.jtr`, a map written in Jestyr itself — runs at
1.37× the speed of its `std::unordered_map` C++ twin (one machine: Windows 11,
gcc/g++ 8.3, -O2, medians; byte-identical outputs; timings are local, see
[Performance](performance.qmd)). The benchmark program contains **zero**
`unsafe` blocks; the map's nine unsafe sites live inside `std/strmap.jtr`,
behind a checked API.

There is also a quieter argument. The bootstrap seed is compiled by two
different C compilers on two operating systems — MinGW gcc on Windows and gcc
13.3.0 on Ubuntu 24.04 — and the resulting compilers re-emit the compiler
byte-for-byte and agree on the determinism canary digest (`4389bf83…`),
pinned by CI on every push. Undefined behaviour is precisely the license for
two compilers to diverge; across ~30K lines of exercised Jestyr, they don't.
That is meaningful evidence against latent UB on the exercised paths — and
only that: UB can hide on untaken paths or coincide across platforms, and
macOS/clang is untested.

::: {.claim}
916 default tests green, a 148-file byte-identical corpus, and the gcc-only
bootstrap fixed point — verified on Windows and Ubuntu CI. Scope: byte-identity
is the single-file/concat emission path; correctness is cross-platform via CI,
timings are one machine.
<span class="verify">$ cargo test --features c-oracle,selfhost-fixpoint</span>
:::

## Honest scope

The escape guarantee is a precise claim with an informal exhaustiveness
argument, validated empirically at compiler scale — it is **not a mechanized
proof**. A formalization is future work, and
[docs/escape-guarantee.md](https://github.com/AdamEzzat1/Jestyr/blob/master/docs/escape-guarantee.md) states exactly the
theorem it would prove, alongside what the claim does not cover: `genref`
faults at runtime rather than compile time, `region` and `unsafe` make their
own explicit promises, and the guarantee is about lifetimes, not data races.
The rejection demos (`examples/escapes.jtr`, `examples/collection.jtr`,
`examples/region_escape.jtr`) keep every route firing, in the test suite, on
every push.
